text: And last, adding a new look later. The React version is longer than the plain one. The React docs admit it. The React code, quote, "Is longer than the original imperative example, but it is much less fragile." Here is what less fragile means in practice. Suppose the shop's server could later answer that a code has expired. In React, we add one more value to the list, the string expired. We add one more line of JSX. It shows this code has expired when status is expired. The other looks do not change at all. The docs say this way of working lets you later introduce new visual states without breaking existing ones. In the plain version, every handler would need one more hide command for the new line. Three later lessons go further. Lesson twenty-two covers in full which values should not be state at all. Lesson twenty-seven moves the logic of many looks into a reducer. And lessons forty-one to forty-four show React.19 form actions, which give you a waiting flag without a handmade status. And here's the last card, Principle five: Handlers set state. The handler names the next look, and React changes the page. Make each handler call a setter and nothing else on the page. Let the JSX decide what is turned off, shown, hidden, or styled for each look. Old habits die hard. [laughs] You reach for getElementById inside a React handler because it is quicker and it seems to work. Then the server says no, and the button stays off forever. You see, React only changes what is different between its last render and its new one, and your handmade change is not in either of them. So never edit the page behind React's back. Call the setter for the next look, and React will turn things on and off for you. The box shows it in two tiny handlers. The one to follow calls preventDefault, then setStatus with checking, and its note says, "The JSX for checking turns the box and Apply off." The one to avoid calls preventDefault, then getElementById on applyButton and sets disabled to true. Its note says it is wrong. React never turns this button back on. Now the synthesis, putting all five principles together. First, the complete project files. Here are the files of our React page. The fake server answers after one and a half seconds. We start with the fake server itself in src/checkcode.js. It exports one function, checkCode, which takes the code and returns a promise. Inside, a setTimeout waits fifteen hundred milliseconds. Then, if the code is the string welcome, the promise resolves. Any other code and it rejects with a new error that says, "This code is not valid." The stylesheet holds the classes for both versions of the page. The stylesheet hasn't changed. Index.css, still the same three rules. The class hidden gets display: none; the class error gets the color red; and the class code-box--error gets a border: two pixels solid red. The entry file mounts App into the root div of index.html. What does main.jsx actually do? Not much, and that's the point. It imports StrictMode from React, createRoot from react-dom-client, our App component, and the stylesheet. Then on line six, it calls createRoot on document.getElementById 'root' and renders App wrapped inside StrictMode. The main file renders one promo code box. App.jsx is even shorter. It imports PromoCode from the components folder, and the App function returns one PromoCode tag. That's all. The promo code box holds the two pieces of essential state, one handler that only sets the next look and JSX that describes every look. And this is where all five principles live in PromoCode.jsx. Line five is principle four, the text in the box, code and setCode from useState with an empty string. Line six is principle four again, one string for the look, status and setStatus starting at the string typing. Then line eight is principle two. The success look has no form. If status is success, the component returns only a paragraph. "Code applied. You get free delivery." Now the handler, handleSubmit. It calls preventDefault, then setStatus with the string checking. That's principle three, a human input. Then it awaits checkCode. If that works, setStatus success. Principle three, a computer input, yes. And in the catch, setStatus error. A computer input, no. Notice the handler never touches an element. The JSX does all of that. On line twenty-seven, the input's class name is computed from state. That's principle five. Code box with the error class when status is error and plain code box otherwise. The input's value is code. Its onChange calls setCode, and it's disabled while status is checking. The Apply button is disabled when the code is empty or while checking. And at the bottom, a checking line appears only while checking, and the line, "This code is not valid," appears only on error. Next, how React calls the components. When the page opens, React starts at App, and App renders the promo code box. On every later change, only the promo code box draws again because only its state changed. Picture a small tree read from the top down. That's Figure thirty-three. At the top sits main.jsx. It mounts App into the root div, and it runs once when the page loads. Below it, step one, App, it's called first, and it returns the promo code tag. Then step two, PromoCode. It's called second and again after every setter call. For typing, checking, and error, it returns the form. For success, it returns only the success line. So the figure shows the order in which React calls the components and what the promo code box returns for each look.
